passage:
Ten days before the semester exams at the agricultural college in Ludhiana district, Gurleen had stopped doing anything except study. She read the same page on soil nitrogen four times and remembered none of it. Her head felt stuffed with cotton.
Her friend Vijay found her in the hostel reading room. "You look terrible. Kabaddi on the back field at six. One hour. Come."
"I don't have time for games."
"You don't have time not to."
She went, grumbling. For an hour she ran, shouted, fell in the dust and laughed so hard at Vijay's clumsy raid that her stomach hurt.
Back in her room, showered, she opened the soil nitrogen page. This time it made sense on the first read. She finished the chapter by ten.
The next day she wrote "6 pm: kabaddi" in her timetable, in ink.

qa.q: What time did Vijay say kabaddi was?
qa.a: Vijay said kabaddi on the back field at six.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling before she went to play?
qa.a: Gurleen felt stressed and foggy, her head stuffed with cotton, and guilty about taking time off.

qa.q: What did Gurleen learn, and how did she act on it?
qa.a: She learned that an hour of play helped her mind recover, so she wrote "6 pm: kabaddi" in her timetable in ink.

qa.q: How does Vijay see play during exam time?
qa.a: Vijay sees it as necessary, not wasted, which is why he says Gurleen doesn't have time not to play.

grounding: A stressed student schedules an hour of kabaddi and finds her mind returns sharper, showing play is a recovery tool.

passage:
It was raining hard in Bengaluru, and Bhavna's plan for a lazy Sunday with friends had shrunk to two hours before everyone's next thing. She noticed it as they sat at Varun's flat.
Varun was showing them his pottery. "I'm going to start selling on a craft site. If I post daily, I can hit a thousand followers by March."
Rukmini said her running was about beating her pace. Arvind had turned his guitar into a video channel with a schedule.
Bhavna felt tired just listening. When had any of them done something just because it was fun, and badly?
She took a sheet of paper and a crayon from Varun's niece's box. "Rule: we draw the rain. Terribly. No photos. No posting."
Varun laughed. "Why?"
"Because nobody's counting."
For forty minutes they drew wobbly clouds and argued about purple rain. Varun's was the worst. He was grinning the whole time.

qa.q: How many followers did Varun hope to reach by March?
qa.a: Varun hoped to hit a thousand followers by March.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling as her friends described their hobbies?
qa.a: Bhavna felt tired and a little sad, noticing that none of them did anything just for fun anymore.

qa.q: What small step did Bhavna take, and why might it help?
qa.a: She set up a no-posting, draw-it-badly game, which let everyone play purely for fun and rest from constant goals.

qa.q: How did Varun experience drawing the rain?
qa.a: Varun enjoyed it and relaxed, grinning the whole time even though his drawing was the worst.

grounding: A young adult notices friends turn every hobby into a metric and starts a purely-for-fun game, reclaiming play.

passage:
At the community centre in Chennai, Jatin sat through the residents' meeting with five-year-old Karthik beside him. After ten minutes Karthik tugged his sleeve.
"Appa, there's nothing to do."
"We'll go soon."
"I'm BORED." He climbed onto Jatin's lap and hung on his neck.
Jatin didn't hand him his phone. He whispered, "I don't know what to do either. What could you do with that paper cup?"
Karthik frowned at the cup. Then he started turning it into a hat. Then a telescope.
By the end of the meeting, he was spying on the committee members through it.

qa.q: What did Karthik turn the paper cup into?
qa.a: He started turning it into a hat, then a telescope.

qa.q: Why did Karthik cling to Jatin's neck?
qa.a: Karthik felt bored and restless, and didn't yet know how to find something to do on his own.

qa.q: What did Jatin do that helped Karthik get past his boredom?
qa.a: Instead of giving his phone, Jatin asked what Karthik could do with the paper cup, nudging him to invent his own activity.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been feeling during the meeting?
qa.a: Jatin was likely a little stressed about keeping Karthik quiet, then relieved and amused to see him playing with the cup.

grounding: A child says there is nothing to do and clings to a parent, and a gentle nudge helps him generate his own activity.

passage:
The power went off at noon in their Jaipur colony and didn't come back all afternoon. No fan, no television, no charging the tablet. Siddharth, ten, lay on the floor and moaned, "There's NOTHING to do."
His sister Bhavna, fourteen, was reading. "Then do nothing."
He did nothing for twenty minutes. It was awful. Then he looked at the bedsheets, the dining chairs, and the broom.
By three o'clock there was a fort in the living room, with a sheet roof and a flag made from a pencil and a sock. By four, he had invented a game called "Fort Defence" with rules written on a notebook page, and Bhavna had joined as the attacking army.
When the power came back at six, the TV blinked on. Siddharth didn't look. "Wait, we haven't finished the siege."

qa.q: What did Siddharth use for the fort's flag?
qa.a: The flag was made from a pencil and a sock.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel during the twenty minutes of doing nothing?
qa.a: Siddharth felt bored and restless, finding the empty time awful before ideas began to come.

qa.q: Why did the power cut turn out well for Siddharth?
qa.a: Without screens, he had to sit through boredom, and that is where the fort and his own game grew.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have seen her brother's fort by the end?
qa.a: Bhavna likely found it fun and impressive enough to join in as the attacking army.

grounding: Left without screens on a long afternoon, a child moves through boredom to build a fort and invent a game.

passage:
I'm Vikas, Gargi's Papa, and for a long time I handed her the tablet the moment she said "I'm bored." It seemed kind. It was quiet.
Then one Sunday I noticed something. She didn't even want the tablet; she wanted the boredom to stop. The second it was in her hands, her face went blank.
So the next time she said it, I said, "Hmm. That's a hard feeling. You'll figure something out," and went back to cooking.
She sulked. She followed me around. She lay on the floor saying "Papa, PLEASE." I nearly gave in.
Twenty minutes later it went quiet. I peeked. She had lined up all her stuffed toys and was holding a school, with a register and a tiny chalkboard she'd drawn on cardboard.
Now I wait a bit before rescuing her. She usually rescues herself.

qa.q: What did Gargi make her chalkboard from?
qa.a: She drew a tiny chalkboard on cardboard.

qa.q: What did Vikas realise about handing Gargi the tablet?
qa.a: Vikas felt uneasy when he noticed her face go blank, realising she only wanted the boredom to stop, not the tablet itself.

qa.q: What change did Vikas make, and why did it help?
qa.a: He named the feeling, didn't rush to fill it and waited, which gave Gargi room to invent her own game.

qa.q: What was the wait like for Gargi?
qa.a: Gargi felt frustrated and bored at first, sulking and pleading, then absorbed and happy running her toy school.

grounding: A parent notices that rescuing a child from boredom with a tablet teaches outside filling, and a short wait brings creativity.

passage:
It was a Sunday afternoon in Barcelona, and Nour, fifteen, lay on her bed with her phone. Video app. Swipe. Photo app. Swipe. Back to the video app. The same flat feeling followed her through every one.
She had homework, a book half-read, a guitar in the corner. It wasn't that there was nothing to do. It was that the quiet felt unbearable, like an itch, and the phone scratched it for a second.
Her friend Alejandro texted: "want to walk to the park?"
She almost said no. Then she noticed her thumb had opened the same app three times in a minute.
"ok," she typed.
At the park they sat on a bench without phones, watching an old man feed pigeons. For the first few minutes Nour kept reaching for her pocket. Then, slowly, she stopped. The flat feeling eased.

qa.q: How many times had Nour's thumb opened the same app in a minute?
qa.a: Her thumb had opened the same app three times in a minute.

qa.q: What was Nour feeling as she switched between apps?
qa.a: Nour felt restless and flat, as though the quiet were an unbearable itch the phone only scratched for a second.

qa.q: What helped Nour, and what could she try again?
qa.a: Noticing her own scrolling and choosing a phone-free walk with a friend; she could try sitting through a few empty minutes without reaching for the phone.

qa.q: How might Alejandro have seen the afternoon at the park?
qa.a: Alejandro probably enjoyed the calm time together and may have noticed Nour slowly relaxing.

grounding: A teenager scrolls compulsively to escape a flat feeling, showing boredom as intolerance for an empty moment.

passage:
At the agricultural college in the small town, Zubin sat in Farm Machinery class and felt his eyes close. It was the third week in a row.
After class he sat with his friend Hrithik under the neem tree. "I'm so bored in that class. Maybe I'm just lazy."
Hrithik shrugged. "Is it too simple for you? Too tough? Or you just don't care?"
Zubin thought. It wasn't too hard; he'd scored well in the quiz. It wasn't too easy either; he couldn't repair the tractor they practised on. "I think I don't see why I'd ever use it. I want to work on seeds and soil, not engines."
"So that's not lazy. That's information."
Zubin looked at the elective list that evening. Seed Science had space. He switched the next week, and stayed awake for every class.

qa.q: Which elective did Zubin switch to?
qa.a: Zubin switched to Seed Science.

qa.q: What was Zubin worried about when he said he might be lazy?
qa.a: Zubin felt anxious and ashamed that his boredom meant a flaw in him rather than a mismatch with the course.

qa.q: What question helped Zubin, and why?
qa.a: Hrithik asked whether the class was too easy, too hard or meaningless to him, which turned boredom into information that guided his choice.

qa.q: How did Hrithik see Zubin's boredom?
qa.a: Hrithik didn't judge it as laziness; he saw it as a useful signal worth reading.

grounding: A student reads his boredom in a course as data, asks whether it is too easy, too hard or meaningless, and chooses better.

passage:
Nursery note for Leela's mother, Maria
Leela skipped her nap today because of the noise from the painting next door. By three she cried over a crayon, threw her shoe, then clung to my leg. Asked what was wrong, she just wailed.
She was very tired.
I held her in the quiet corner with her blanket and she slept in minutes. She woke up smiling.
Please let her sleep early tonight.

qa.q: Why did Leela skip her nap?
qa.a: Leela skipped her nap because of the noise from the painting next door.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she cried and clung?
qa.a: Leela was overtired and upset, too worn out to say why she felt so bad.

qa.q: What worked for Leela, and why?
qa.a: Holding her in a quiet corner with her blanket so she could sleep, since tiredness, not naughtiness, was behind her behaviour.

qa.q: How might Maria see Leela's evening after reading the note?
qa.a: Maria might feel reassured and understanding, seeing any crankiness as tiredness and planning an early bedtime.

grounding: A caregiver's note shows an overtired toddler becoming tearful and clingy, and a nap fixing what discipline could not.

passage:
Monday. At bedtime Afreen begged for "one more story", then another, then water, then a trip to the window. "What if you and Abbu eat ice cream after I sleep?" Neelam got cross. Afreen cried herself to sleep at ten.
Wednesday. Neelam started a routine: bath, pyjamas, two stories, a song, lights off. She put the steps on a card with pictures. "Same every night."
Afreen checked the card at each step. "Two stories. Then song."
Saturday. After the song, Afreen yawned. "Ammi, you'll be here in the morning?"
"Right here. And no ice cream without you."
Afreen giggled and was asleep before nine.

qa.q: What steps were on Neelam's picture card?
qa.a: Bath, pyjamas, two stories, a song, lights off.

qa.q: What was Afreen worried about on Monday?
qa.a: Afreen was afraid of missing out, worried her parents would eat ice cream once she was asleep.

qa.q: Why did the routine help Afreen?
qa.a: A predictable, calm routine showed her what came next and that sleep didn't mean being left out.

qa.q: What was bedtime like for Neelam on Monday?
qa.a: On Monday Neelam felt cross and worn out as Afreen kept stalling, and bedtime ended in tears.

grounding: A child fights bedtime from fear of missing out, and a predictable routine with a calm ending teaches that rest is safe.

passage:
In their Nairobi house, Wanjiru, nine, lay on the sofa after school with a comic. Her father came in and sighed. "Lying around again? Look at your uncle Otieno. Up at five, two jobs, never sits down. That's how you get ahead."
Wanjiru sat up quickly and pretended to look for her homework. Her cheeks burned. Resting felt like something she had to hide.
That weekend her aunt Nour visited. After lunch, Nour stretched out on the veranda mat. "Come, Wanjiru. Rest with me. We've both worked hard this week."
Wanjiru hesitated. "Isn't that lazy?"
"Resting isn't lazy. It's how you have energy for the good things," Nour said, closing her eyes. "Even Otieno sleeps."
Wanjiru lay down beside her. The sun was warm. For the first time in weeks, she didn't feel guilty for stopping.

qa.q: How many jobs does uncle Otieno have?
qa.a: Uncle Otieno has two jobs.

qa.q: Why did Wanjiru's cheeks burn when her father spoke?
qa.a: Wanjiru felt ashamed, as though resting were something bad she had to hide.

qa.q: What could a parent say instead to respect a child's downtime?
qa.a: Something like Nour's words: resting after school isn't lazy, it's how you get energy for the good things.

qa.q: How does Nour see rest?
qa.a: Nour sees rest as normal and earned, relaxing openly and inviting Wanjiru to rest without guilt.

grounding: A child told resting is lazy while a busy adult is praised feels ashamed, and an aunt who respects downtime helps her stop without shame.
